name: Vit D3
description: Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) contributes to the normal absorption of calcium and phosphorus and helps maintain normal bones, teeth, and muscle function. Public Health England and the NHS recommend that all adults and children over four take a daily supplement of 10 micrograms (400 IU) during autumn and winter, and that people at risk of low sun exposure — including those with dark skin, those who cover their skin, and people who are housebound — take 10 micrograms year-round. The safe upper limit for adults is 100 micrograms (4,000 IU) per day; exceeding this may cause harmful levels of calcium to build up in the body. D3 is the form the body naturally produces via sunlight and is widely considered the preferred supplemental form.

name: Vit C
description: Vitamin C contributes to the normal function of the immune system, the protection of cells from oxidative stress, and the maintenance of normal skin, blood vessels, bones, and cartilage. The UK recommended intake for adults is 40 mg per day, which most people can achieve through a varied diet rich in fruit and vegetables; however, a supplement may be useful if dietary intake is insufficient. The NHS advises keeping supplement doses below 1,000 mg per day, as higher amounts can cause stomach pain, diarrhoea, and flatulence. Unlike some vitamins, vitamin C cannot be stored in the body, so consistent daily intake is needed.

name: Vit B Complex
description: A vitamin B complex supplement contains a combination of B vitamins — typically B1 (thiamine), B2 (riboflavin), B3 (niacin), B5 (pantothenic acid), B6, B7 (biotin), B9 (folate), and B12 — each of which contributes to normal energy-yielding metabolism and the reduction of tiredness and fatigue. B vitamins are water-soluble and cannot be stored in the body (except B12), so regular intake from food or supplements is important, particularly for people with restricted diets. The NHS notes that most people get sufficient B vitamins through a balanced diet, but those following a vegan diet, older adults, and people with certain medical conditions may benefit from supplementation. Each constituent vitamin has its own safe upper limit; follow label directions and do not exceed stated doses.

name: Vit B12
description: Vitamin B12 contributes to normal red blood cell formation, normal neurological function, and normal energy-yielding metabolism. The UK reference nutrient intake (RNI) for adults is 1.5 micrograms per day, though B12 occurs naturally only in animal products, making vegans and strict vegetarians particularly at risk of deficiency. The NHS specifically recommends that vegans take a B12 supplement or consume B12-fortified foods regularly. Taking 2 mg or less per day from supplements is considered unlikely to cause harm.

name: Folic Acid
description: Folic acid (the synthetic form of folate, vitamin B9) contributes to the normal formation of red blood cells and plays a critical role in cell division during pregnancy. The NHS recommends that all women who are pregnant or planning to become pregnant take 400 micrograms of folic acid daily until the end of the 12th week of pregnancy to reduce the risk of neural tube defects such as spina bifida; women with a higher risk (e.g., a family history of neural tube defects or those taking certain medicines) are advised to take a higher dose of 5 mg daily under GP supervision. The safe upper limit from supplements is 1 mg per day for the general adult population; exceeding this can mask symptoms of a vitamin B12 deficiency. All adults require 200 micrograms of folate daily from dietary sources.

name: Vit A
description: Vitamin A (retinol) contributes to the normal function of the immune system, the maintenance of normal vision in dim light, and healthy skin and mucous membranes. The UK recommended intake is 700 micrograms per day for men and 600 micrograms for women, and the body stores any surplus in the liver. The NHS and the Department of Health and Social Care warn that consuming more than an average of 1,500 micrograms daily over many years may increase the risk of bone fractures, particularly in older adults and postmenopausal women; pregnant women are advised to avoid all high-dose vitamin A supplements and liver products due to the risk of harm to the developing baby.

name: Vit E
description: Vitamin E contributes to the protection of cells from oxidative stress and supports the normal function of the immune system. Men need approximately 4 mg per day and women 3 mg per day, amounts that are readily available from a diet containing vegetable oils, nuts, seeds, and wheatgerm. The Department of Health and Social Care advises that taking 540 mg (800 IU) or less of vitamin E per day from supplements is unlikely to cause harm; the body stores any excess, so daily supplementation is not essential if dietary intake is adequate.

name: Vit K
description: Vitamin K is essential for normal blood clotting and contributes to the maintenance of normal bones. Adults need approximately 1 microgram per kilogram of body weight daily (e.g., 65 micrograms for a 65 kg adult), and most people can often obtain this from green leafy vegetables, vegetable oils, and cereal grains. The NHS advises that taking 1 mg or less per day from supplements is unlikely to cause harm; however, people taking anticoagulant medicines such as warfarin must consult their GP before taking any vitamin K supplement, as it can significantly affect how those medicines work.

name: Biotin
description: Biotin (vitamin B7) contributes to normal energy-yielding metabolism, the maintenance of normal hair and skin, and the normal functioning of the nervous system. It is produced in small amounts by bacteria naturally present in the gut, and good sources include eggs, meat and nuts. The NHS considers taking 0.9 mg or less per day from supplements unlikely to cause harm; very high doses of biotin supplements have also been reported to interfere with certain laboratory blood tests, so it is advisable to inform your healthcare provider if you are supplementing.

name: Niacin
description: Niacin (vitamin B3) contributes to normal energy-yielding metabolism, the reduction of tiredness and fatigue, and the maintenance of normal skin and nervous system function. The UK recommended intake is 16.5 mg per day for men and 13.2 mg for women; good dietary sources include meat, fish, wheat flour, eggs, and milk. The NHS advises keeping nicotinic acid (one form of niacin) supplements to no more than 17 mg per day, as higher doses can cause skin flushing and, with prolonged high-dose use, potential liver damage; nicotinamide (the other form) has a higher safe limit of 500 mg per day.

name: Vit B5
description: Pantothenic acid (vitamin B5) contributes to normal energy-yielding metabolism and the normal synthesis and metabolism of steroid hormones, vitamin D, and some neurotransmitters. There is no established UK recommended daily intake, as it is widely found in many foods including chicken, beef, eggs and deficiency is extremely rare. The NHS considers taking 200 mg or less per day from supplements unlikely to cause harm.

name: Riboflavin (B2)
description: Riboflavin (vitamin B2) contributes to normal energy-yielding metabolism, the maintenance of normal skin and mucous membranes, and the normal functioning of the nervous system and eyes. The UK recommended intake is 1.3 mg per day for men and 1.1 mg for women; good sources include milk, eggs, fortified cereals, and lean meats. The NHS advises taking 40 mg or less per day from supplements; riboflavin is light-sensitive, so foods rich in it should be stored away from direct sunlight.

name: Thiamine (B1)
description: Thiamine (vitamin B1) contributes to normal energy-yielding metabolism and the normal function of the heart and nervous system. The UK recommended intake is 1 mg per day for men and 0.8 mg for women, and it is found in peas, fresh and dried fruit, eggs, wholegrain breads, and some fortified cereals. Because thiamine is water-soluble and cannot be stored in the body, a regular daily intake is needed; the NHS considers taking 100 mg or less per day from supplements to be unlikely to cause harm.

name: Vit C + Zinc Combos
description: This combination tablet provides both vitamin C and zinc, two nutrients that each contribute to the normal function of the immune system. Vitamin C also contributes to the protection of cells from oxidative stress and normal collagen formation, while zinc contributes to normal protein synthesis and the maintenance of normal vision. The NHS recommends keeping vitamin C supplements below 1,000 mg per day and zinc supplements to no more than 25 mg per day from supplements; taking zinc above this limit can reduce copper absorption and may lead to anaemia over time.

name: Multivitamins
description: A multivitamin tablet provides a broad range of vitamins and minerals in a single dose, designed to help fill nutritional gaps where dietary intake may be insufficient. The NHS notes that most people who eat a varied and balanced diet do not need a multivitamin; however, specific groups — including pregnant women (who need folic acid and vitamin D), adults over 65, people with restricted diets, and those with limited sun exposure — may benefit. Care should be taken to avoid double-dosing on individual nutrients when taking a multivitamin alongside other supplements, particularly for fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K.

name: Vit K2
description: Vitamin K2 (menaquinone) is a form of vitamin K that contributes to normal blood clotting and normal bone maintenance; some research suggests it may have a specific role in directing calcium to bones rather than soft tissues, though this is an area of ongoing study. The NHS notes that most people can obtain sufficient vitamin K from a balanced diet including green vegetables, fermented foods, and some animal products. As with all forms of vitamin K, people taking anticoagulant drugs (e.g., warfarin) should seek medical advice before supplementing, as even small changes in vitamin K intake can alter the effectiveness of these medicines; the general safe upper limit from supplements is 1 mg per day.

name: Magnesium Tablets
description: Magnesium contributes to the reduction of tiredness and fatigue, normal muscle and nerve function, normal protein synthesis, and the maintenance of normal bones and teeth. The UK recommended intake is 300 mg per day for men and 270 mg for women, The NHS advises that taking no more than 400 mg per day from supplements is unlikely to cause harm; higher doses may cause diarrhoea.

name: Magnesium Glycinate
description: Magnesium glycinate is a chelated form of magnesium — magnesium bound to the amino acid glycine — which is often noted for its higher bioavailability and gentler effect on the digestive system compared to other forms such as magnesium oxide. Magnesium contributes to normal muscle and nerve function, normal psychological function, and the maintenance of normal bones. As with all magnesium supplements, the NHS recommends limiting intake from supplements to no more than 400 mg per day to avoid adverse effects such as diarrhoea.

name: Magnesium Citrate
description: Magnesium citrate is a form of magnesium combined with citric acid, commonly chosen for its relatively good solubility and absorption. Magnesium contributes to normal energy-yielding metabolism, normal functioning of the nervous system, and the maintenance of normal bones and teeth. The NHS advises that no more than 400 mg per day of magnesium from supplements should be taken by adults; higher doses are associated with digestive side effects including diarrhoea.

name: Iron Supplements
description: Iron contributes to the normal formation of red blood cells and haemoglobin, normal oxygen transport in the body, and the reduction of tiredness and fatigue. The UK recommended intake is 8.7 mg per day for men and postmenopausal women, and 14.8 mg per day for women of childbearing age due to menstrual losses. The NHS advises that supplements providing 17 mg or less per day are unlikely to cause harm; however, taking more than 20 mg can cause constipation, nausea, and stomach pain — very high doses are dangerous, particularly for children. Iron supplements should only be taken long-term on medical advice, as excess iron can be harmful.

name: Zinc Supplements
description: Zinc contributes to the normal function of the immune system, normal protein synthesis, the maintenance of normal skin and hair, and normal wound healing. The UK recommended intake is 9.5 mg per day for men and 7 mg for women, obtainable from red meat, shellfish, dairy, seeds, and pulses. The NHS advises not exceeding 25 mg per day from supplements, as higher intakes can reduce the body's absorption of copper and over time may lead to copper deficiency and anaemia.

name: Calcium Supplements
description: Calcium contributes to the maintenance of normal bones and teeth, normal muscle function including heartbeat regulation, and normal blood clotting. Adults aged 19 and over need 700 mg per day, which most can meet through dairy products, fortified plant milks, leafy green vegetables, and sardines eaten with bones. The NHS advises that taking 1,500 mg or less per day from supplements is unlikely to cause harm; exceeding this amount may lead to stomach pain, diarrhoea, and in rare cases an increased risk of kidney stones.

name: Selenium
description: Selenium contributes to the normal function of the immune system, the protection of cells from oxidative stress, and normal thyroid function. The UK recommended intake is 75 micrograms per day for men and 60 micrograms for women; Brazil nuts are an exceptionally rich source, though intake can vary widely. The NHS advises keeping selenium from supplements to no more than 350 micrograms per day, as higher doses can cause selenosis — symptoms of which include hair loss, nail changes, and nerve damage.

name: Potassium Supplements
description: Potassium contributes to the normal function of the nervous system and muscles, and helps maintain normal blood pressure. Adults need 3,500 mg per day, which is readily obtainable from bananas, potatoes, pulses, nuts, and vegetables; most healthy adults do not need to supplement. The NHS advises caution in older adults, who should only take potassium supplements under medical supervision as impaired kidney function can lead to dangerously high blood potassium levels (hyperkalaemia); the general safe upper limit from supplements is 3,700 mg per day.

name: Copper
description: Copper contributes to the normal function of the immune system, the maintenance of normal connective tissue, and the normal transportation of iron in the body. The UK recommended intake for adults is 1.2 mg per day, found in shellfish, nuts, seeds, and wholegrains. The NHS advises that the combined intake from food, water, and supplements should not exceed 10 mg per day, as excessive copper intake can cause liver damage; those taking high-dose zinc supplements should be particularly mindful, as zinc competes with copper for absorption.

name: Chromium
description: Chromium contributes to the normal macronutrient metabolism and helps the body maintain normal blood glucose levels by supporting insulin function. The UK reference intake for adults is 25 micrograms per day, obtainable from meat, wholegrains, vegetables, and some spices. The NHS advises that the total intake from food and supplements combined should not exceed 10 mg per day; most people eating a balanced diet are unlikely to be deficient.

name: Iodine
description: Iodine contributes to the normal production of thyroid hormones and normal thyroid function, which in turn supports normal energy metabolism. Adults need 140 micrograms per day, primarily from dairy products, eggs, and white fish; people following a vegan diet excluding these foods may have lower intakes and should consider a supplement or fortified foods after seeking advice from a healthcare professional. The NHS advises taking no more than 0.5 mg (500 micrograms) per day from supplements; excess iodine can disrupt thyroid function just as deficiency can.

name: Boron
description: Boron plays a role in supporting normal bone and joint metabolism, and some research suggests it may assist in the utilisation of vitamin D and magnesium. Boron is not formally classified as an essential nutrient in UK dietary reference values, and there is currently no established recommended daily intake from the Department of Health and Social Care. Boron supplements are subject to The Food Supplements (England) Regulations 2003; consumers should follow product label guidance and not exceed manufacturer recommendations, typically no more than 3 mg per day.

name: Manganese
description: Manganese contributes to normal energy-yielding metabolism, the maintenance of normal bones, and the normal formation of connective tissue. A specific UK recommended daily amount has not been set, as intakes from a varied diet containing wholegrains, nuts, and leafy vegetables are generally considered sufficient. The NHS advises that adults should not take more than 4 mg of manganese per day from supplements, with a lower limit of 0.5 mg per day for older adults; very high intakes over time may affect the nervous system.

name: Ashwagandha
description: Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) is an adaptogenic (stress-relief) herb with a long history of use in Ayurvedic medicine, traditionally used to support the body's response to stress and to support energy levels. It is regulated in the UK as a food supplement under The Food Supplements (England) Regulations 2003 and cannot make medicinal claims without a product licence. Some clinical trials suggest potential benefits for perceived stress and sleep quality, but the evidence base is still emerging and the MHRA has not granted a Traditional Herbal Registration (THR) for this herb. Consumers should follow label dosing guidance, and people with autoimmune conditions, thyroid disorders, or those taking prescription medicines should consult a GP before use.

name: Gingko Biloba
description: Ginkgo biloba is a botanical supplement derived from the leaves of the ginkgo tree, traditionally used to support circulation and cognitive function; it is one of the most studied herbal supplements worldwide. In the UK it is sold as a food supplement and cannot make medicinal claims; some products have been granted a Traditional Herbal Registration (THR) by the MHRA for the relief of symptoms of Raynaud's syndrome or mild memory impairment associated with ageing. Ginkgo biloba can interact with anticoagulant and antiplatelet medicines such as warfarin and aspirin, increasing the risk of bleeding, so people taking such medications should consult their GP before use.

name: St Johns Wort
description: St John's Wort (Hypericum perforatum) is a herbal remedy that has been used for centuries and is available in the UK as a Traditional Herbal Registered (THR) medicine — indicated for the relief of slightly low mood and mild anxiety, based on traditional use. St John's Wort is known to interact with a wide range of medicines including antidepressants, oral contraceptives, anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin), HIV medications, and some heart medicines, and these interactions can be serious; consumers should always consult a pharmacist or GP before use if taking any other medication.

name: CBD Oil
description: Cannabidiol (CBD) oil is derived from the hemp plant (Cannabis sativa) and is subject to Novel Foods authorisation requirements in the UK; consumers should only purchase products that are linked to a valid application on the Food Standards Agency (FSA) CBD products register. The FSA currently advises that healthy adults consume no more than 10 mg of CBD per day as a food supplement and recommends that CBD products are not used by children, pregnant or breastfeeding women, or people taking prescription medicines without first consulting a doctor or pharmacist. CBD products do not contain significant levels of THC (the psychoactive compound in cannabis) and are not classified as controlled substances when compliant with UK law, but the evidence base for health benefits remains under scientific review.

name: L-Theanine
description: L-theanine is an amino acid found naturally in tea leaves (Camellia sinensis), best known for its association with a calm but alert state of mind; it is commonly consumed in combination with caffeine for cognitive support. In the UK it is sold as a food supplement and is not subject to any specific UK government recommended daily intake guidance, but it has been assessed as safe by EFSA. Most supplement doses range from 100–400 mg per day; individuals sensitive to amino acids, those taking blood pressure medications, or those with liver conditions should seek medical advice before use.

name: Lion's Mane Mushroom
description: Lion's Mane (Hericium erinaceus) is an edible mushroom used in traditional East Asian medicine and now sold as a food supplement in the UK; it is of interest for its potential to support nerve growth factor (NGF) pathways and cognitive function, though human clinical evidence is currently limited. It is regulated as a food supplement in the UK under The Food Supplements (England) Regulations 2003, meaning it cannot make claims to treat or prevent disease. Consumers should purchase from reputable sources to ensure quality, as supplement standards can vary; individuals with mushroom allergies or those on anticoagulant therapy should seek medical advice before use.

name: Omega-3 Fish Oil
description: Omega-3 fish oil provides long-chain omega-3 fatty acids, primarily EPA (eicosapentaenoic acid) and DHA (docosahexaenoic acid), which contribute to the normal function of the heart at a daily intake of 250 mg of combined EPA and DHA. The NHS recommends eating at least one portion (approximately 140 g cooked) of oily fish per week as the preferred dietary source; a supplement may be appropriate for those who do not eat fish. Fish liver oil supplements (such as cod liver oil) differ from fish body oil supplements in that they also contain high levels of vitamins A and D, and pregnant women are advised to avoid fish liver oil supplements due to the risk of excess vitamin A.

name: Triple Omega 3,6,9
description: Triple omega supplements combine omega-3 (from fish or plant oils), omega-6 (typically from evening primrose or borage oil), and omega-9 (typically from olive or sunflower oil) fatty acids. Omega-3 fatty acids (EPA/DHA) contribute to normal heart function at intakes of 250 mg per day; omega-6 linoleic acid is an essential fatty acid widely available in the UK diet and deficiency is rare. Omega-9 (oleic acid) is a non-essential monounsaturated fat the body can make itself; EFSA has not established specific authorised health claims for combined omega supplements, and most people in the UK get sufficient omega-6 and omega-9 through their diet. The combined supplement should be taken as directed on the label.

name: Coenzyme Q10
description: Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10, also known as ubiquinone) is a substance made naturally by the body and found in the mitochondria of cells, where it plays a key role in producing cellular energy (ATP). Natural levels of CoQ10 decline with age and may also be reduced by statin medications, which is why some people on statins take CoQ10 supplements, though the NHS notes that evidence for this use remains inconclusive. In the UK, CoQ10 is sold as a food supplement under The Food Supplements (England) Regulations 2003 and cannot claim to treat any medical condition; it is generally considered safe at doses up to 200 mg per day, but anyone on blood-thinning medicines or diabetes medication should consult a GP before use.

name: Garlic Supplements
description: Garlic (Allium sativum) has a long tradition of use for supporting circulation and cardiovascular wellness, and some research suggests its active compound allicin may contribute to maintaining normal blood lipid levels and blood pressure, though evidence from large clinical trials is mixed. In the UK, garlic is sold as a food supplement and cannot claim to treat or cure heart disease; some products with Traditional Herbal Registration (THR) status from the MHRA are authorised for use as a traditional herbal remedy to relieve symptoms of upper respiratory catarrh. Garlic supplements can interact with anticoagulant medicines including warfarin, increasing bleeding risk, so people taking blood-thinning medicines should consult their GP before use.

name: Krill Oil
description: Krill oil is extracted from Antarctic krill (Euphausia superba) and provides omega-3 fatty acids (EPA and DHA) in phospholipid form, as well as the antioxidant astaxanthin; these omega-3 fatty acids contribute to the normal function of the heart at a daily intake of 250 mg of combined EPA and DHA. Some research suggests the phospholipid form may have higher bioavailability than the triglyceride form found in standard fish oil, though evidence comparing clinical outcomes is still limited. Krill oil is regulated as a novel food in Great Britain and people with shellfish or seafood allergies should avoid krill oil supplements.

name: Resveratrol
description: Resveratrol is a polyphenol antioxidant (stress-reliever) found naturally in red grapes, berries, and peanuts, and is of scientific interest for its potential to support cardiovascular health and cellular protection from oxidative stress. In the UK it is regulated as a food supplement under The Food Supplements (England) Regulations 2003; EFSA has reviewed resveratrol and has not authorised any specific health claims due to insufficient human clinical evidence at this time. Most commercial supplements provide 50–500 mg per day; resveratrol may interact with blood-thinning medicines and certain medications metabolised by the liver, so people on prescription drugs should consult a GP before use.

name: Algae Based Omega 3
description: Algae-based omega-3 supplements provide DHA (docosahexaenoic acid) and sometimes EPA (eicosapentaenoic acid) derived from marine microalgae — the original dietary source of these fatty acids in the marine food chain — making them a suitable option for people following vegetarian or vegan diets. DHA contributes to the maintenance of normal brain function and normal vision at a daily intake of 250 mg, and EPA and DHA together contribute to normal heart function at 250 mg per day. EFSA has authorised these claims, and the NHS recommends that those who do not eat oily fish consider algae-based omega-3 as an alternative source of long-chain omega-3 fatty acids.

name: Beetroot Capsules
description: Beetroot is a rich dietary source of inorganic nitrate, which the body converts to nitric oxide — a compound that contributes to the widening of blood vessels and normal blood flow. Some research, including studies referenced in UK sports science literature, suggests concentrated beetroot supplements may support exercise performance and healthy blood pressure; however, EFSA has not authorised a specific health claim for beetroot at this time. Beetroot capsules are regulated as a food supplement in the UK and cannot make cardiovascular or blood pressure treatment claims; most products provide the equivalent of one to two beetroots per serving, and they are considered safe for most adults when taken as directed.

name: Hawthorn Berry
description: Hawthorn (Crataegus monogyna/oxyacantha) berries and extracts have been used in European herbal medicine for centuries to support cardiovascular wellness and normal circulation. In the UK, some hawthorn products have been granted a Traditional Herbal Registration (THR) by the MHRA, authorising their traditional use for the relief of temporary tiredness and sensations of heart palpitations — based on long-standing traditional use rather than clinical evidence. Hawthorn may interact with prescribed heart medicines and blood pressure drugs; consumers on any cardiac medication should always consult their GP or pharmacist before using hawthorn supplements.

name: Whey Protein Powder
description: Whey protein is a high-quality complete protein derived from cow's milk during the cheese-making process, providing all essential amino acids and contributing to the growth and maintenance of muscle mass when consumed alongside resistance exercise. The NHS advises that most people in the UK get enough protein from their diet (the UK RNI is 0.75 g per kg of body weight per day for adults), and protein supplements are generally unnecessary for those who are not engaged in high levels of athletic training. Whey protein is not suitable for people with a cow's milk allergy or lactose intolerance; high-protein diets and supplements should be avoided by those with kidney disease unless under medical supervision.

name: Plant Based Protein
description: Plant-based protein powders — commonly made from pea, rice, hemp, or soy protein — provide a vegan and vegetarian-friendly alternative to whey, contributing to the growth and maintenance of muscle mass when consumed alongside adequate resistance exercise. Protein contributes to a growth in muscle mass and maintenance of muscle mass per EFSA authorised health claims; individual plant protein sources may have a slightly lower digestibility score than animal proteins, though blending sources (e.g., pea and rice) can improve the amino acid profile. People with soy or other legume allergies should check ingredient lists carefully; as with all protein supplements, those with kidney disease should seek medical advice before use.

name: Creatine
description: Creatine is a naturally occurring compound stored primarily in muscle tissue, where it plays a key role in rapid energy production (ATP resynthesis) during short bursts of high-intensity exercise; supplementation with creatine monohydrate is one of the most researched performance supplements available. EFSA has concluded that creatine supplementation contributes to an increase in physical performance during successive bursts of short-term, high intensity exercise, based on a daily intake of 3 g. Creatine is generally considered safe for healthy adults; however, people with kidney disease or pre-existing kidney conditions should consult a GP before use, and it should not be taken by children or adolescents without medical supervision.

name: Electrolytes
description: Electrolyte powders typically provide a blend of key minerals — most commonly sodium, potassium, magnesium, and calcium — that are lost through sweat during exercise and are essential for normal fluid balance, nerve conduction, and muscle contraction. These minerals each have EFSA-authorised health claims for contributing to normal electrolyte balance, normal muscle function, and normal nerve function. Electrolyte supplements are particularly useful for athletes exercising for more than one hour or in hot environments; healthy adults who do not exercise intensively can generally meet electrolyte needs through a balanced diet and adequate fluid intake and people who intermittently fast to restore minerals.

name: Amino Acid
description: Amino acid supplements provide individual or blended essential and non-essential amino acids — the building blocks of proteins — to support muscle repair, recovery, and protein synthesis. Essential amino acids, including branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs) such as leucine, isoleucine, and valine, must be obtained from the diet as the body cannot synthesise them; protein contributes to the growth and maintenance of muscle mass per EFSA authorised health claims. Most people consuming adequate dietary protein will obtain sufficient amino acids without supplementation; people with phenylketonuria (PKU) or other metabolic conditions affecting amino acid processing must follow specific medical dietary advice and should not take general amino acid supplements without GP guidance.

name: Collagen Blends
description: Collagen is the most abundant protein in the human body, forming the structural basis of skin, bones, tendons, and cartilage; collagen supplement blends — typically hydrolysed bovine or marine collagen — are marketed to support skin elasticity and joint comfort. EFSA has not yet issued an authorised health claim specifically for collagen supplementation, and the evidence base in humans — particularly regarding whether orally consumed collagen peptides are absorbed intact to reach target tissues — is still developing. Collagen powders are regulated as food supplements in the UK; people with fish or shellfish allergies should check the source of marine collagen carefully, and those following halal or kosher diets should verify the origin of bovine collagen.

name: Beta-Alanine
description: Beta-alanine is a non-essential amino acid that combines with histidine in muscle tissue to form carnosine, a compound that acts as a buffer against the build-up of lactic acid during intense exercise, potentially helping to maintain performance and reduce fatigue during high-intensity efforts lasting one to four minutes. EFSA has not issued a specific authorised health claim for beta-alanine; however, it is one of the more evidence-backed sports nutrition ingredients with multiple human clinical trials supporting its ergogenic effects. A common and harmless side effect of beta-alanine supplementation is a temporary tingling sensation in the skin (paraesthesia), particularly with doses above 800 mg; this can be reduced by taking smaller, divided doses throughout the day.

name: Probiotics + Prebiotics
description: Probiotics are live bacteria and yeasts that, when consumed in adequate amounts, may contribute to the normal balance of gut microbiota; prebiotics are dietary fibres that selectively feed beneficial gut bacteria. The NHS notes that some evidence suggests certain probiotic strains may help ease symptoms of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), and they are generally considered safe for healthy adults with an intact immune system. In the UK, probiotics are classified as food supplements rather than medicines, meaning they are not subject to the same rigorous clinical evidence requirements; efficacy varies by strain, dose, and individual, and health claims for specific outcomes require EFSA authorisation. People with compromised immune systems or serious underlying conditions should consult a GP before taking probiotic supplements.

name: Apple Cider Vinegar
description: Apple cider vinegar (ACV) is made from fermented apple juice and has been used traditionally as a folk remedy for digestive discomfort; in tablet form it provides a standardised, convenient alternative to liquid ACV without the associated tooth enamel erosion risk. Currently, EFSA has not authorised any specific health claims for apple cider vinegar, and the NHS notes that there is limited good-quality clinical evidence to support the many claims made for ACV as a health supplement. ACV is regulated as a food supplement in the UK; liquid ACV can erode tooth enamel and irritate the oesophagus, so dilution must be considered when drinking — and very high doses may interact with diuretic medicines or insulin.

name: L-Glutamine
description: L-glutamine is the most abundant amino acid in the body and plays a key role in gut lining integrity, immune cell function, and nitrogen transport between tissues; it is classified as conditionally essential, meaning the body's own production may become insufficient during periods of illness, intense exercise, or recovery from surgery. In the UK it is sold as a food supplement under The Food Supplements (England) Regulations 2003 and cannot make medicinal claims; it is used by some athletes to support gut health and muscle recovery after prolonged training. L-glutamine is generally considered safe at doses up to 14 g per day in healthy adults; people with liver cirrhosis, kidney disease, or seizure disorders should not take glutamine supplements without medical advice.

name: Aloe Vera Capsules
description: Aloe vera is a succulent plant whose gel has been used traditionally in many cultures for digestive and skin wellness; in capsule form, standardised aloe vera extracts are commonly taken to support digestive comfort and normal bowel function. The NHS notes that the evidence for aloe vera as a digestive supplement is limited; importantly, anthraquinone-containing aloe latex (found in the outer leaf) is not the same as the inner gel, and high doses of anthraquinone compounds have been associated with adverse effects including diarrhoea and, in animal studies, carcinogenicity. In the UK, the European Commission has prohibited the use of aloe emodin and related anthraquinones from food supplements; consumers should ensure products are labelled as aloe vera inner leaf gel (decolorised) and follow recommended label doses.

name: Slippery Elm
description: Slippery elm (Ulmus rubra) is derived from the inner bark of the North American elm tree and has been used in traditional herbal medicine for centuries to soothe and coat the lining of the mouth, throat, stomach, and intestines. In the UK it is regulated as a food supplement; some products have Traditional Herbal Registration (THR) status from the MHRA authorising their use as a traditional remedy for the relief of sore throat and digestive discomfort. Slippery elm is high in mucilaginous fibre and may slow the absorption of other medications taken at the same time; it is advisable to take it at least two hours apart from any prescription medicines.

name: Skin Hair and Nails
description: Skin, hair, and nails combination supplements typically provide a blend of nutrients with EFSA-authorised health claims for these specific body systems, including biotin (which contributes to the maintenance of normal hair and normal skin), zinc (which contributes to the maintenance of normal skin, hair, and nails), vitamin C (which contributes to normal collagen formation for normal skin), and selenium (which contributes to the maintenance of normal nails and normal hair). Deficiency in any of these nutrients can contribute to changes in hair, skin, and nail quality, though in the absence of a true nutritional deficiency, the additional benefit of supplementation for cosmetic improvement is not well established in clinical evidence.

name: Glucosamine + Chondroitin
description: Glucosamine and chondroitin are structural components of cartilage naturally found in the body; they are commonly taken together in supplement form by people looking to support joint comfort and mobility. The NHS notes that some people with osteoarthritis report that glucosamine supplements help ease their symptoms. These supplements are generally considered safe for most adults; however, glucosamine is derived from shellfish in most formulations, which is relevant to people with seafood allergies, and people with diabetes should monitor blood glucose levels as glucosamine may affect insulin sensitivity.

name: MSM
description: MSM (methylsulfonylmethane) is an organic sulphur compound found in small amounts in many foods, including fruits, vegetables, grains, and milk; sulphur is an important component of several amino acids and plays a structural role in collagen, cartilage, and connective tissue. MSM is commonly taken alongside glucosamine and chondroitin for joint support. It is regulated as a food supplement in the UK under The Food Supplements (England) Regulations 2003; typical doses in studies are 1,500–3,000 mg per day and it is generally considered well-tolerated.

name: Calcium + Vit D + Magnesium Combos
description: This three-way combination tablet provides calcium, vitamin D, and magnesium — three nutrients that work synergistically to support the maintenance of normal bones and teeth. Calcium is the primary structural mineral of bone (adults need 700 mg/day); vitamin D is essential for normal calcium absorption (10 micrograms/day recommended by the NHS); and magnesium contributes to normal protein synthesis and bone maintenance (300 mg/day for men, 270 mg/day for women). The NHS recommends this combination particularly for older adults at risk of osteoporosis, though supplementation should complement — not replace — a balanced diet; do not exceed 1,500 mg calcium, 100 micrograms vitamin D, or 400 mg magnesium from supplements per day.

name: Turmeric
description: Turmeric (Curcuma longa) is a culinary spice containing the active polyphenol curcumin, which has attracted significant scientific interest for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties in laboratory studies. In the UK, turmeric is sold as a food supplement under The Food Supplements (England) Regulations 2003 and cannot claim to treat, prevent, or cure conditions such as arthritis; EFSA has not authorised a specific health claim for curcumin at this time. Curcumin has poor bioavailability on its own, which is why many supplements are formulated with piperine (black pepper extract) to enhance absorption; people taking anticoagulant medicines (e.g., warfarin), diabetes medication, or those due for surgery should consult their GP before use.

name: Devil's Claw
description: Devil's Claw (Harpagophytum procumbens) is a southern African plant root traditionally used in European herbal medicine to relieve mild joint and back pain; in the UK, some Devil's Claw products have been granted Traditional Herbal Registration (THR) by the MHRA, permitting their authorised use for the temporary relief of backache, rheumatic or muscular pain, and general aches and pains in muscles and joints, based on traditional use. THR products bear the THR logo and have been assessed for quality and safety, though efficacy evidence is based on traditional use rather than clinical trials. Devil's Claw may interact with anticoagulant medicines and antacids, and is not recommended during pregnancy; always consult a pharmacist if taking other medicines.

name: Children's Multivitamin Gummies
description: Children's multivitamin gummies are designed to provide a range of vitamins in a palatable format for children who may not get all nutrients from their diet. The NHS recommends that all children aged 6 months to 5 years take a daily supplement containing vitamins A, C, and D, as these are the nutrients most likely to be insufficient in young children's diets; children eligible for the Healthy Start programme can obtain free vitamin drops from their health visitor. Gummy supplements typically contain added sugars, so dental hygiene after consumption is important; parents should always follow the age-appropriate dosing instructions on the label and avoid giving multiple supplements simultaneously, as this can lead to excessive intake of fat-soluble vitamins.

name: Baby Liquid Multivitamin Drops
description: Liquid vitamin drops for babies are specifically formulated to provide vitamins A, C, and D in a safe, age-appropriate liquid dose that can be added to food or dropped directly into the mouth. The NHS recommends vitamin drops containing these three vitamins for all breastfed babies from birth onwards, as breast milk alone may not provide sufficient vitamin D (and vitamin A and C in some cases); babies who drink more than 500 ml of infant formula per day do not need additional vitamins as formula is already fortified. The standard recommended dose of vitamin D for babies is 8.5–10 micrograms per day; parents should not exceed stated doses as excessive intake of vitamins A and D can be harmful to infants.

name: Vitamin D3 Drops
description: Vitamin D3 drops provide cholecalciferol in a liquid format suitable for infants, young children, and adults who have difficulty swallowing tablets. The NHS recommends that breastfed babies from birth, and all children aged 1–4 years, take a daily supplement of 8.5–10 micrograms of vitamin D; adults should consider 10 micrograms daily during the autumn and winter months, and year-round if they have limited sun exposure, dark skin, or are housebound. Care should be taken to use an appropriately calibrated dropper to avoid exceeding the safe upper limit: 25 micrograms per day for infants under 12 months, 50 micrograms for children aged 1–10, and 100 micrograms for adults.

name: Elderberry Syrup
description: Elderberry (Sambucus nigra) is a berry with a long tradition of use in European folk medicine, particularly for supporting the immune system during the winter cold and flu season; it is regulated in the UK as a food supplement and cannot make claims to prevent or treat viral infections. Some small clinical studies suggest elderberry extract may contribute to reduced duration of cold symptoms, though the evidence is not yet sufficient for EFSA to authorise a specific health claim. Raw elderberries and elderberry seeds contain cyanogenic glycosides (sambunigrin) which can cause nausea; commercial elderberry syrups are processed to make them safe, but consumers — particularly parents giving syrups to children — should purchase from reputable brands and always follow age-appropriate dosing on the label.

name: Choline
description: Choline is an essential nutrient that contributes to normal lipid metabolism and the maintenance of normal liver function. The UK has not established a formal RNI for choline, but adequate intake levels are considered to be 400 mg per day for adults and higher during pregnancy (450 mg) and breastfeeding (550 mg), where it is important for foetal brain development. Choline is found in eggs, meat, fish, dairy, and cruciferous vegetables; supplementation is generally considered safe at doses up to 3.5 g per day, though higher intakes may cause a fishy body odour, low blood pressure, and sweating.

name: Evening Primrose Oil
description: Evening primrose oil (EPO) is derived from the seeds of Oenothera biennis and is a rich source of gamma-linolenic acid (GLA), an omega-6 fatty acid that the body uses to produce anti-inflammatory prostaglandins. It is commonly used by women for breast pain (mastalgia), symptoms of premenstrual syndrome (PMS), and menopausal discomfort; some products have Traditional Herbal Registration (THR) from the MHRA for the relief of breast pain associated with the menstrual cycle. The overall evidence from clinical trials is mixed; the NHS notes that EPO is unlikely to cause serious harm when taken as directed, but it may interact with blood-thinning medicines and could lower the seizure threshold in people with epilepsy.

name: DIM
description: DIM (diindolylmethane) is a compound produced in the body from the digestion of indole-3-carbinol, found naturally in cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli, cauliflower, and Brussels sprouts; it is thought to support healthy oestrogen metabolism by promoting the production of less potent oestrogen metabolites. In the UK, DIM is sold as a food supplement under The Food Supplements (England) Regulations 2003 and cannot make hormonal treatment claims; EFSA has not issued an authorised health claim for DIM. Because DIM affects oestrogen pathways, women who are pregnant, breastfeeding, or taking hormone-based contraceptives or HRT should consult their GP before use; standard supplement doses are typically 100–300 mg per day.

name: Maca Root
description: Maca (Lepidium meyenii) is a Peruvian root vegetable traditionally consumed as food and used in folk medicine to support energy, libido, and hormonal balance; it is classified as a food supplement in the UK under The Food Supplements (England) Regulations 2003 and cannot make medicinal claims. Some human clinical trials suggest maca may help support sexual function and menopausal well-being, though EFSA has not issued an authorised health claim for maca at this time due to insufficient evidence. Maca is generally considered safe when taken in amounts consistent with its use as a food; people with thyroid conditions should exercise caution as maca contains glucosinolates which may affect thyroid function, and pregnant or breastfeeding women should seek medical advice before use.

name: Saw Palmetto
description: Saw palmetto (Serenoa repens) is a small palm native to North America whose berry extract is commonly used to support urinary tract comfort in men, particularly in relation to symptoms associated with a normal ageing prostate. In the UK, saw palmetto is regulated as a food supplement under The Food Supplements (England) Regulations 2003; some European products have obtained registration for traditional use in relation to lower urinary tract symptoms, though EFSA has not issued an authorised health claim. Men experiencing significant urinary symptoms should always consult their GP to rule out underlying medical conditions before using any supplement.

name: Tribulus
description: Tribulus terrestris is a plant used in traditional Ayurvedic and Chinese medicine; it is commonly marketed in the UK as a men's supplement for supporting testosterone levels and physical performance, though clinical evidence for significant effects on testosterone in healthy men is limited and inconsistent. EFSA has not issued an authorised health claim for tribulus, and it is regulated as a food supplement in the UK under The Food Supplements (England) Regulations 2003 — meaning it cannot claim to treat hormonal conditions or enhance testosterone. Men on heart medicines, diabetes medication, or those with hormone-sensitive conditions should consult their GP before use.

name: Zinc + Magnesium (ZMA)
description: ZMA is a combination supplement providing zinc, magnesium, and vitamin B6, formulated to support normal testosterone levels, muscle recovery, and sleep quality in physically active individuals. Zinc contributes to the maintenance of normal testosterone levels in the blood and normal protein synthesis; magnesium contributes to a reduction in tiredness and fatigue and normal muscle function; and vitamin B6 contributes to normal protein and glycogen metabolism — all EFSA-authorised claims. The NHS recommends not exceeding 25 mg of zinc or 400 mg of magnesium per day from supplements; ZMA is intended for adults and should not be taken alongside other zinc or magnesium supplements to avoid exceeding safe upper limits.

name: Shilajit
description: Shilajit is a naturally occurring resinous exudate found in the Himalayas and other mountain ranges, traditionally used in Ayurvedic medicine as a rejuvenating tonic; it is rich in fulvic acid and trace minerals. In Great Britain, shilajit is subject to Novel Foods authorisation requirements, meaning it requires assessment and authorisation by the Food Standards Agency (FSA) before it can be legally sold as a food supplement; consumers should check that any product they purchase is linked to a valid FSA novel food application. Because of variability in raw material purity and the potential presence of heavy metals in some unprocessed forms, purchasing from brands with verified third-party testing is strongly advised; people with kidney disease, haemochromatosis, or those on blood-thinning medications should consult a GP before use.

name: Fenugreek
description: Fenugreek (Trigonella foenum-graecum) is a culinary herb and traditional herbal medicine used in South Asian and Middle Eastern cultures; it is commonly taken in the UK as a supplement by men to support testosterone and libido, and by breastfeeding women to support milk production, though clinical evidence for both uses is mixed. It is regulated as a food supplement in the UK under The Food Supplements (England) Regulations 2003 and cannot make hormonal or lactation treatment claims; EFSA has not issued an authorised health claim for fenugreek. Fenugreek may lower blood glucose levels and could interact with diabetes medications and anticoagulants.
